unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 10 is the final unit of Grade 5, and it gathers the whole year into one project. You revise thirty words from Units 1 to 8, from coal, pouch and empire to persuade, rural and citizenship. Six grammar workshops bring back the adjective pairs, the tenses, the questions, the comparisons and the joining words. Then you read five review texts, build a multi-section English product for a real audience, present it, answer questions and reflect on how far you have come.
unit.learningPath:
Read the five review texts and answer the twelve comprehension questions.
Revise the thirty review words and build your word map, unit by unit.
Work through the six grammar workshops, one at a time.
Plan, draft and improve a multi-section product for a real audience.
If you have access to live teacher sessions, rehearse across them and deliver your presentation there — this is optional. If you are learning independently, rehearse and record your presentation on your own or with your family instead.
Answer audience questions, then finish with the capstone quiz, the portfolio assignment and your Grade 6 reflection.

readings.title: Review text 1: The Silence After the Rumble, part 3
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
A season passed, and the courthouse still stood on its cracked foundations.
Amal unlocked the doors every single morning, proud of the small role that opened the court on time.
One misty day a family arrived from one of the distant regions, carrying a folded land paper in a worn pouch.
Suddenly, she encountered a boy her age, who looked anxious and would not meet her eyes.
“My grandfather sent us,” he said. “He is too ill to travel, but he needs the court to hear him.”
Amal did not hesitate. She led the family inside and filled the water jug on the judge’s bench, just as she did each day.
The visiting elder was there again. He listened, then turned to the students. “Justice is slow,” he said, “but it must never forget the smallest citizen.”
The boy whispered to Amal, “Do you decide the cases?”
“No,” she answered. “I only open the doors. Yet without me, nothing here begins.”
That evening Grandma Hana stirred soup over the coal stove. “You carried yourself like a leader today,” she said.
Amal smiled. Two years earlier an earthquake had broken their town, and many families had moved away.
She had stayed, and now she understood why. The court was a promise, and every morning she kept it.

readings.title: Review text 2: The Burrow Discovery, part 3
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
That afternoon Teacher Yasmin gathered the class to hear the blog results.
"The winning team is Amal, Nora and Sami," she announced, and the room erupted.
"You will present at the town library next week," she said when the cheering faded.
"You will also join a local energy project. Your task is to reduce the glare from public lights and consume less electricity."
"Another project?" asked Sami, suddenly feeling drowsy.
"You mustn't nap yet," laughed Nora. "This is a great chance."
The next morning they were walking to the community hall when they saw pupils holding painted signs.
Two of them were struggling to hoist a long banner above the doors.
"What is happening?" asked Amal.
"They are starting a boycott of plastic cups in the lunchroom," Maya explained.
"They want to protect the environment, and they say the waste is a real issue."
"Should we join them?" asked Nora.
"I would rather research it first," said Sami. "Nobody should sign anything they have not read."
So they talked to the group leader, who showed them his figures and a simple contract.
Hundreds of cups were used every week, and none of them were recycled.
"You have our approval," said Amal. "We will help you announce it next week."
"Taking ownership of a problem is the first step," Nora added, signing her name neatly.
The hall was not an ideal meeting place, but it was free and everybody fitted inside.
They wrote one last blog entry that evening, taking turns at the keyboard.
"Today we joined a group of pupils who want to end plastic cups in our lunchroom.
We cooperated, shared ideas and wrote a plan. Not everyone agrees yet, but we are working on it.
We also learned that nothing in science happens quickly, so you have to be patient.
Mix loyalty, effort and curiosity, though, and the results can be brilliant."

readings.title: Review text 3: The Cracked Charter, part 3
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
On exhibition day the class hung their youth charter beside the old cracked one.
Nora read the opening aloud: “We believe nobody is too small to speak, and our mission is to learn, to listen and to lead.”
The mayor came to see the display. She studied the new policy the students had written and their careful comparison of old rules and new ones.
“You have turned a fracture into a foundation,” she said. “One day some of you may serve in our legislative halls.”
“And I will design them,” said Amal. “I want to be an architect.”
“You function well as a team,” the mayor added. “And that’s the most powerful kind of constitution.”
As they left, the cracked charter remained in its case — but now, it had new meaning.
It was no longer only a broken page. It was a lesson that even a crack can lead to something stronger.
Sami looked back once. “A town works better,” he said, “when every citizen is allowed to speak.”
Teacher Yasmin smiled. “That,” she said, “is the finest thing you have written all year.”

readings.title: Review text 4: The Hasty Route, part 3
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Back at camp that night the team compared the two paths by lamplight. Amal wrote in the log:
"Route A was more comfortable, less dangerous, and full of ancient clues. Route B was shorter, but hotter and riskier. The dreadful wind made it miserable."
Noah added a line of his own:
"I was too forceful in my choice. Amal's slower plan was wiser. Her idea to explore carefully led to a profitable find."
Later, around the fire, they sipped warm tea. Leo asked, "Do you think we will be chosen to present at the regional fair?"
"I think we have a good chance," Amal replied. "Our site is unique, and we worked well together."
Noah nodded. "We disagreed, but we kept moving. That is what made it honorable."
The next day the team began preparing their presentation.
"We are writing about the explorers who found Desert Point 4," said Amal.
"And about the decisions that taught them patience," Noah added.
They printed photographs, drew diagrams, and annotated the map. Their report contained one sentence Amal was proud of:
"The storm that delayed us led to a well which had never been recorded before."
At the school fair a judge asked, "Was the storm a mistake?"
"No," Amal replied. "It was part of the journey."
"And would you do it again?" the judge asked.
"Only with this team," she said, smiling. "They are the most faithful, most dutiful, most honorable crew imaginable."

readings.title: Review text 5: The Memory Wall, part 3
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
On Friday, the last day of the Memory Wall, Teacher Yasmin invited a local author to read the pupils' work aloud.
He read Nora's drawing-story and Leo's memory. “I am touched,” he said. “These words are better than many books I have read.” He paused. “Who wrote this one, about the boy who remembered everything he heard?”
Leo raised his hand. “It is mine.”
“Did you know that generations ago, stories travelled only by memory? You have honoured that tradition.”
Leo felt his heart race, and this time it was not fear. It was pride.
At home that night, Leo's younger brother asked, “What is a slave?”
Leo thought carefully before he answered. “A slave is somebody who was forced to work and was not allowed any freedom. But those people still had their own thoughts, their own stories and their own hope.”
“Like Grandpa's story?”
“Yes,” said Leo, smiling. “And now I have written it down, so it will not be forgotten.”
The following week, the Memory Wall came down, but nobody threw it away. Instead, the class turned it into a book.
“Your work will be shared with next year's pupils,” said Teacher Yasmin. “You have built something real.”
“I did not expect that,” said Nora.
“You believed in one another,” said Teacher Yasmin. “You united, didn't you?”
“Definitely,” said Leo. “We did not exaggerate anything. We simply told the truth.”

comprehension.correctAnswer: She understands that opening the courthouse doors each morning is important, because without her nothing there can begin.
comprehension.explanation: The passage ends with Amal seeing that she opens the court, so justice starts on time each day.

comprehension.question: Which detail shows that Amal helps the visiting family straight away?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She does not hesitate; she leads the family inside and fills the water jug on the judge's bench.
comprehension.explanation: The text says Amal did not hesitate and led the family in, showing she acts quickly and kindly.

comprehension.question: Why do Amal, Nora and Sami decide to support the plastic-cup boycott?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The group leader's figures show hundreds of cups are used each week and none are recycled, so the waste is a real issue.
comprehension.explanation: The friends act only after they see the leader's data about wasted, unrecycled cups.

comprehension.question: What does Sami say before the friends agree to sign anything?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He says he would rather research it first, because nobody should sign anything they have not read.
comprehension.explanation: Sami insists on reading and researching before signing, which shows careful, independent thinking.

comprehension.question: What important idea does the mayor share when she looks at the students' work?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She says that a team which works well together is the most powerful kind of constitution.
comprehension.explanation: The mayor praises the students' teamwork and calls it the strongest kind of constitution.

comprehension.question: What does the cracked charter come to mean to the class by the end?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It becomes a lesson that even a crack, or fracture, can lead to a stronger foundation.
comprehension.explanation: The passage closes by saying the cracked charter now means that a fracture can build something stronger.

comprehension.question: What does Noah admit about his earlier choice of route?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He admits he was too forceful, and that Amal's slower, more careful plan was wiser and led to a profitable find.
comprehension.explanation: Noah writes in the log that his forceful choice was wrong and Amal's careful plan was better.

comprehension.question: How does Amal answer the judge who asks whether the storm was a mistake?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She says no, the storm was part of the journey, and it led to a well that had never been recorded before.
comprehension.explanation: Amal tells the judge the storm was part of the journey and produced a valuable discovery.

comprehension.question: Why is Leo proud when the visiting author praises the writing?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The author says Leo has honoured the old tradition of passing stories on by memory, and this time Leo feels pride instead of fear.
comprehension.explanation: The author's praise about honouring memory turns Leo's racing heart from fear into pride.

comprehension.question: What happens to the Memory Wall after it is taken down?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The class turns it into a book that will be shared with next year's pupils.
comprehension.explanation: The passage says the wall was not thrown away but made into a book for future pupils.

comprehension.question: Both this passage and the other review texts show characters growing in confidence. What helps Amal grow here?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Keeping her daily promise to unlock the court, and helping the anxious boy's family, help Amal see herself as a leader.
comprehension.explanation: Amal's steady duty and her kindness to the family are what build her confidence in this text.

comprehension.question: Using this passage, explain why the courthouse matters so much to Amal.
comprehension.correctAnswer: The courthouse is a promise she keeps every morning, and it is where the town decides what is fair for every citizen.
comprehension.explanation: The passage links the courthouse to Amal's daily promise and to fair decisions for every citizen.

grammar.title: Sentence accuracy audit
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Revisit three Grade 5 accuracy targets: complete sentences, the indefinite pronouns from Unit 2, and the adjective-and-preposition pairs from Unit 1.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Every sentence needs a subject and a verb: "Amal presented her board."
Indefinite pronouns take a singular verb: "Everyone is ready." "Nobody knows."
Adjective and preposition pairs stay fixed: proud of, afraid of, good at, interested in.
grammar.commonMistake: Writing "Everyone are ready" or "proud from her work" — match the singular verb and keep the correct preposition.
grammar.memoryTip: Read each sentence and underline its subject and verb before you check the small words around them.
grammar.practice: Part A: fix the verb in six indefinite-pronoun sentences. Part B: correct the preposition in six adjective pairs. Part C: rewrite two fragments from your portfolio as complete sentences. Check yourself: Part A and Part B use your own six indefinite-pronoun sentences and six adjective-and-preposition pairs, so there is no single fixed list to mark against - as a self-check, confirm every indefinite pronoun (everyone, nobody, somebody, everything, and similar words) takes a singular verb such as is, has, knows or does (e.g., "Everyone is ready," not "Everyone are ready"), and that each adjective keeps its fixed partner (proud of, afraid of, good at, interested in), never a swapped preposition like "proud from." Part C is open-ended - model example: a fragment such as "Running to the bus stop." becomes the complete sentence "Amal was running to the bus stop."

grammar.title: Tense control
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Bring together the tenses of the year: the present perfect from Unit 8, the present continuous for future plans from Unit 4, and the zero conditional from Unit 5.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Present perfect: "I have finished my draft."
Present continuous for a plan: "We are presenting on Friday."
Zero conditional: "If you rehearse, you feel calmer."
grammar.commonMistake: Mixing time markers, such as "Yesterday I have presented" — use the simple past with a finished time: "Yesterday I presented."
grammar.memoryTip: Name the time first, then choose the tense that matches it, and keep the whole paragraph in step.
grammar.practice: Part A: choose the correct tense in eight sentences about your capstone. Part B: rewrite four sentences to describe a future plan. Part C: write two zero-conditional rules for your reader. Check yourself: Parts A-C use sentences and rules you write about your own capstone, so there is no fixed list to check against - as a self-check, confirm Part A matches each time marker to its tense (a finished time such as yesterday takes the simple past: "Yesterday I presented"; an unfinished action takes the present perfect: "I have finished my draft"), that Part B uses the present continuous for each future plan (e.g., "We are presenting on Friday"), and that Part C's rules follow the zero-conditional pattern If + present, + present (e.g., "If you rehearse, you feel calmer").

grammar.title: Questions and responses
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Prepare for audience questions by revisiting question forms and the opinion language from Unit 7, so you can agree or disagree politely.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Wh- question: "Why did you choose this topic?"
Yes/no question: "Did the project change your mind?"
Opinion and reply: "I think that the mural matters." "I agree, because it saved a piece of history."
grammar.commonMistake: Answering only "yes" or "no" — add a reason so the listener understands your thinking.
grammar.memoryTip: For every answer, say your point and then your "because", so each reply carries a reason.
grammar.practice: Part A: turn six statements into Wh- questions. Part B: write one polite agreement and one polite disagreement. Part C: answer four likely audience questions in full sentences. Check yourself: Part A turns your own six statements into Wh- questions - as a self-check, confirm each new question starts with a Wh- word (Why, What, How, When, Where or Who) and keeps the auxiliary verb in front of the subject, matching the pattern "Why did you choose this topic?" Part B is open-ended - model example: agreement - "I agree, because the mural saved a piece of history"; disagreement - "I see your point, but I think the new mural also matters." Part C is open-ended - model example: for the question "Why did you choose this topic?" a full-sentence answer is "I chose this topic because it connects to our town's history."

grammar.title: Description and precision
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Sharpen your describing language with the comparatives and superlatives from Unit 3, the adjective order and similes from Unit 8, and the compound nouns from Unit 9.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Comparative and superlative: "clearer than before," "the clearest page."
Adjective order: "a small old wooden box."
Simile: "as bright as sunlight."
Compound noun: "notebook, courtroom, woodland."
grammar.commonMistake: Doubling a comparison, such as "more clearer" — choose either the -er ending or the word "more," never both.
grammar.memoryTip: Add one precise word at a time and read the sentence aloud; stop as soon as the picture is clear.
grammar.practice: Part A: complete six comparative and superlative sentences. Part B: order the adjectives in four noun phrases. Part C: build four compound nouns and use two similes in your captions. Check yourself: Parts A and B use your own six comparative/superlative sentences and four noun phrases, so as a self-check confirm each comparison uses either the -er ending or the word "more" but never both ("clearer than before," not "more clearer"), each superlative uses -est or "most" ("the clearest page"), and each noun phrase orders adjectives toward the noun as opinion, size, age, then material (e.g., "a small old wooden box"). Part C is open-ended - model example: compound nouns "notebook, courtroom, woodland, sunlight" and a simile in a caption such as "The lake was as bright as sunlight."

grammar.title: Joining ideas
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Link your sentences smoothly using the conjunctions from Unit 6, the relative clauses from Unit 4, and the time connectives from Unit 5.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Coordinating: "We planned, and we rehearsed."
Subordinating: "We revised because the feedback helped."
Relative clause: "the page that I liked best."
Time connective: "First, next, after that, finally."
grammar.commonMistake: Starting formal writing with "And" or "But" — use a connective adverb such as "However" or "Therefore" instead.
grammar.memoryTip: Join two short ideas only when they belong together; if the link feels forced, keep them as separate sentences.
grammar.practice: Part A: combine six sentence pairs with a conjunction. Part B: add a relative clause to four nouns. Part C: order a paragraph using four time connectives. Check yourself: Parts A and B use your own six sentence pairs and four nouns, so there is no fixed list to check against - as a self-check, confirm each combined sentence uses a coordinating conjunction (and, but, so) to join equal ideas ("We planned, and we rehearsed") or a subordinating conjunction (because, although, when) to add a reason or condition ("We revised because the feedback helped"), and that each relative clause starts with who, which or that and sits right after the noun it describes ("the page that I liked best"). Part C is open-ended - model example: a paragraph ordered "First, we chose our topic. Next, we drafted the pages. After that, we revised them. Finally, we presented our work."

grammar.title: Final editing conference
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)
grammar.explanation: Bring every target together in one proofreading pass over your capstone product, checking meaning, grammar, punctuation and layout.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Read once for meaning, once for grammar, once for spelling and punctuation, and once aloud for flow.
grammar.commonMistake: Editing everything at once and missing errors — give each read a single, clear job.
grammar.memoryTip: Change your reading colour or read the last line first, so tired eyes notice what they usually skip.
grammar.practice: Part A: run the four-pass checklist on one page. Part B: log three edits and explain each one. Part C: read the final piece aloud to a partner and note two more fixes. Check yourself: Parts A-C are a personal editing conference on your own capstone page, so there is no fixed answer key - as a self-check, confirm you gave each of the four passes (meaning, grammar, spelling/punctuation, and reading aloud for flow) its own read rather than mixing them, that each of your three logged edits names what was wrong and why the fix improves the sentence (for example, "changed 'have' to 'has' so the verb agrees with 'everything'"), and that after reading aloud to a partner you noted two further fixes based on what sounded unclear.

quizzes.question: What does 'coal' mean?
quizzes.options: A small soft bag that holds little things | A hard black rock that people burn for heat and energy | Areas or parts of a country that share something in common together | A problem that people discuss and try to solve
quizzes.correctAnswer: A hard black rock that people burn for heat and energy
quizzes.explanation: Coal is a black rock we burn to make heat and electricity.

quizzes.question: What does 'pouch' mean?
quizzes.options: A very large area of land that is ruled by one single government | A written rule that guides a group's choices | A restless mood when people feel unhappy | A small soft bag or pocket used to hold little things
quizzes.correctAnswer: A small soft bag or pocket used to hold little things
quizzes.explanation: A pouch is a small bag; the family carried a paper inside a worn pouch.

quizzes.question: What does 'independence' mean?
quizzes.options: To share information or ideas with other people | A group of words that someone has said or written | Being able to look after yourself and make your own choices | Surprising and sudden, because it was not planned or predicted at all
quizzes.correctAnswer: Being able to look after yourself and make your own choices
quizzes.explanation: Independence means making your own choices, as Amal did at the court.

quizzes.question: What does 'issue' mean?
quizzes.options: A problem or topic that people discuss because it needs solving | A city or busy town rather than the countryside | The open countryside, with farms, wide fields and very few buildings around | Extremely angry, so calm is hard to keep
quizzes.correctAnswer: A problem or topic that people discuss because it needs solving
quizzes.explanation: The wasted plastic cups were an issue the students wanted to fix.

quizzes.question: What does 'policy' mean?
quizzes.options: A young sheep, or the meat that comes from it | Feeling worried or nervous about something soon | The quiet countryside, with farms, open fields and very few buildings | A plan or rule that guides the choices a group makes
quizzes.correctAnswer: A plan or rule that guides the choices a group makes
quizzes.explanation: A policy is a guiding rule, like a school policy about spelling.

quizzes.question: What does 'lobby' mean?
quizzes.options: Done too quickly, without thinking it through | A large open area inside a building where people wait | To make someone agree by giving good reasons | The ability to learn, to understand and to think about things carefully
quizzes.correctAnswer: A large open area inside a building where people wait
quizzes.explanation: The class met the curator in the museum lobby.

quizzes.question: What does 'hasty' mean?
quizzes.options: Having plenty of room, so nothing feels crowded | Unwilling, or feeling unsure about doing something | Done too quickly, without stopping to think carefully | A special document that grants certain rights or rules to a whole group
quizzes.correctAnswer: Done too quickly, without stopping to think carefully
quizzes.explanation: A hasty route once led the explorers into danger.

quizzes.question: What does 'reluctant' mean?
quizzes.options: Unwilling, or feeling unsure about doing something | A restless mood when people are unhappy and protest | To uncover something hidden, or make a fact known | Belonging to a city or busy town
quizzes.correctAnswer: Unwilling, or feeling unsure about doing something
quizzes.explanation: Sami was reluctant to sign until he had read every line.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from 'Review text 1: The Silence After the Rumble, part 3': Suddenly, she _____ a boy her age.
quizzes.explanation: The text says: Suddenly, she encountered a boy her age. To encounter is to meet by chance.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from 'Review text 3: The Cracked Charter, part 3': “And that’s the most powerful kind of _____.” As they left, the cracked charter remained in its case.
quizzes.explanation: The text says: And that’s the most powerful kind of constitution.

teacherNotes.note: This capstone reviews Units 1-9, so conference at each milestone and keep the learner's ownership of the product. Ensure an adult is present whenever learners record audio or present online. The thirty review words are drawn from the units as follows: coal, pouch, encounter and regions from Unit 1; independence, issue, empire and expose from Unit 2; policy, lobby, constitution and charter from Unit 3; hasty, reluctant, furious and anxious from Unit 4; communicate, quote, emphasize and persuade from Unit 5; unrest, uneasy, unexpected and unsuccessful from Unit 6; local, urban, rural and spacious from Unit 7; and intelligence and citizenship from Unit 8. Every capstone vocabulary slug matches a word its unit actually taught, so none was revised out. The six grammar workshops revisit the year's targets: adjective-and-preposition pairs and indefinite pronouns; the present perfect, present continuous for future and zero conditional; question and opinion language; comparatives, adjective order, similes and compound nouns; conjunctions, relative clauses and time connectives; and a final editing pass. The five review texts are the closing parts of the Unit 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 stories, using the same cast the learners already know. Assess the multi-section product and presentation with the shared writing and speaking rubrics, and record actionable Grade 6 transition feedback.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Confirm the learner selected one reading, one writing and one speaking piece from Units 1-9 and gave a reason for each choice.
Check that all thirty review words are grouped into sensible categories and that the learner can explain at least two of the links.
Verify the product has a clear audience, a title and at least three connected sections suited to that audience.
Confirm the learner gave two specific rubric-based suggestions and recorded two suggestions they received.
Check the presentation was rehearsed twice and that pace, volume and transitions improved between the two runs.
Confirm the learner presented, answered at least two audience questions and recorded one Grade 6 learning goal.

A large open area inside a building where people wait — The class met the curator in the museum lobby.
